title: Federation: decide peer authentication on the open internet
description: draft-atwood-jmap-chat-federation requires the local server to verify the remote's authenticated identity equals the ownerUserId in its /.well-known/jmap Session, but doesn't say how off a tailnet. Options: mutual TLS bound to the peer's domain, HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) with keys published at the peer's well-known URL, or something else. Decision first, then a spec change in jmap-chat-spec; this blocks federation code.
notes:
Analysis 2026-10-18 (decision still Mark's; spec change in jmap-chat-spec pending).
Options considered:
1. No peer auth (early-SMTP style): rejected. Anyone can claim senderUserId; the draft's anti-spoof rule needs a verified caller.
2. mTLS with WebPKI/Let's Encrypt client certs: likely not viable. Let's Encrypt has been removing the TLS Client Authentication EKU from its certs (Chrome root program change), believed complete in 2026 — VERIFY dates before relying on this. A private federation CA re-centralizes trust.
3. RECOMMENDED: WebPKI (e.g. Let's Encrypt) as trust anchor for key discovery + signed requests. Each server publishes its signing public key in its /.well-known/jmap Session (served over normal HTTPS). Senders sign every Peer/* request with RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures. Receivers fetch the key from https://<sender-domain>/.well-known/jmap (standard cert validation), cache it, verify. Verified identity = controller of HTTPS at that domain; plugs into the draft's existing check of authenticated identity against the peer Session's ownerUserId. Precedent: ActivityPub (HTTP Signatures), Matrix (server keys + signed requests); DKIM is the email analogue (key in DNS instead of HTTPS). Signatures travel with the message, so stored messages remain verifiable.
4. Fallback: XMPP-style dialback (receiver calls the sender's domain back to confirm). No keys, but a round trip per message and no durable proof; stopgap only.
Open details for the spec text: key format and rotation (multiple keys with ids, overlap window), which components the signature covers (method, target URI, content-digest, date/created), clock skew and replay window, key cache TTL and refetch on unknown keyid.

Amendment 2026-10-18 (PKIX/DANE): one identity rule, peer = domain, with two ways to prove it.
- Baseline (MUST): RFC 9421 signed Peer/* requests, signing key fetched from https://<domain>/.well-known/jmap (WebPKI-validated HTTPS, e.g. Let's Encrypt).
- Stronger binding (MAY; SHOULD where DNSSEC is available): publish the same signing key in DNSSEC-signed DNS (TLSA, or a DKIM-style TXT record) so receivers can verify without trusting the public CA system. A valid DANE binding takes precedence over the HTTPS-published key.
- Alternative transport-level mode (MAY): mutual TLS where the sending server presents a client certificate (may be self-signed, PKIX X.509) verified against the sender domain's DNSSEC-signed TLSA record. Avoids the WebPKI clientAuth-EKU problem and needs no federation CA. Precedent: DANE for SMTP between MTAs (RFC 7672); IETF DANCE WG work on DANE for TLS client auth (draft-ietf-dance-client-auth) — CHECK current status (draft vs RFC) before citing.
- Cost: DNSSEC deployment is partial and receivers need a validating resolver, so DANE cannot be the only path; the HTTPS baseline keeps federation open to unsigned domains.
